facts.statement: Gnathosaurus is a genus of ctenochasmatid pterosaur that includes two species, G. subulatus and G. macrurus.
facts.quote: Gnathosaurus (meaning "jawed lizard") is a genus of ctenochasmatid pterosaur containing two species: G. subulatus, named in 1833 from the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany, and G. macrurus, known from the Purbeck Limestone of the UK.

facts.statement: The skull of Gnathosaurus subulatus was slender, measuring 28 cm in length, and featured up to 130 needle-like teeth arranged along a spoon-shaped tip.
facts.quote: This slender, 28 cm long skull had up to 130 needle-like teeth arranged around the side of a spoon-shaped tip.

facts.statement: Gnathosaurus jaw fragments were first found in 1832 in southern Germany but were initially misidentified as a crocodile jaw and named Crocodilus multidens.
facts.quote: Fragments of Gnathosaurus jaws were first discovered in 1832 in the Solnhofen limestones of southern Germany but were mistaken for a piece of teleosaurid crocodile jaw by Georg zu Münster, who first named the species Crocodilus multidens in that year.

facts.statement: A more complete adult skull was discovered in 1951 and classified as Gnathosaurus subulatus.
facts.quote: A more complete skull of an adult pterosaur was found in 1951 and classified as Gnathosaurus subulatus.

facts.statement: A large specimen originally named Pterodactylus macrurus was found in the Purbeck Limestone of England.
facts.quote: An additional large specimen, originally named Pterodactylus macrurus, is known from the Purbeck Limestone formation of England.

facts.statement: Gnathosaurus belongs to the family Ctenochasmatidae.
Gnathosaurus is classified within the subfamily Gnathosaurinae.
Gnathosaurus fossils date back to the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Its fossil remains dated back to the Late Jurassic period.

facts.statement: Gnathosaurus lived between 168.2 and 137.05 million years ago, from the Bathonian to the Berriasian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Berriasian (168.2 to 137.05 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is conjectured that Gnathosaurus used its teeth to filter water and capture small animals.
facts.quote: Los dientes pueden haber sido usados para filtrar agua y capturar pequeños animales, aunque esto es una conjetura.

facts.statement: Bennett (2025) concluded that Aurorazhdarcho micronyx is a junior synonym of Gnathosaurus subulatus based on comparisons with juvenile specimens.
facts.quote: However, Bennett (2025) compared fossil material of Gnathosaurus subulatus with skulls of the largest juvenile specimens of Aurorazhdarcho micronyx, and concluded that Aurorazhdarcho micronyx is indeed a junior synonym of Gnathosaurus subulatus.

facts.statement: Scientists like Albert Oppel concluded that Gnathosaurus was a flying reptile rather than a crocodilian.
facts.quote: Scientists such as Albert Oppel compared the G. subulatus jaw fragment to contemporary pterosaurs such as Pterodactylus and Ctenochasma, and concluded that it was also probably a "flying reptile" rather than a crocodilian.

rejected.quote: It probably lead a lifestyle akin to that of modern spoonbills, wading with its jaws open and closing them upon touching small prey.
